documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.statement:
Lactic acid is formed in the muscles during intense activity (anaerobic metabolism). In the blood, lactic acid is neutralized by reaction with hydrogen carbonate. This will be illustrated by the following calculations:

Lactic acid, written as HL, is monoprotic, and the acid dissociation constant is $K_{\mathrm{HL}}=1.4\times10^{-4}$.

The acid dissociation constants for carbonic acid are $K_{a1}=4.5\times10^{-7}$ and $K_{a2}=4.7\times10^{-11}$. All carbon dioxide remains dissolved during the reactions.

parts.statement: Calculate pH in a $3.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of HL.
Calculate the value of the equilibrium constant for the reaction between lactic acid and hydrogen carbonate.

$3.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of lactic acid (HL) is added to $1.00\ \mathrm{dm}^3$ of $0.024\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ (no change in volume, HL completely neutralized).

i) Calculate the value of pH in the solution of $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ before HL is added.

ii) Calculate the value of pH in the solution after the addition of HL.

pH in the blood of a person changed from $7.40$ to $7.00$ due to lactic acid formed during physical activity. Let an aqueous solution having $\mathrm{pH}=7.40$ and $[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]=0.022$ represent blood in the following calculation. How many moles of lactic acid have been added to $1.00\ \mathrm{dm}^3$ of this solution when its pH has become $7.00$?

In a saturated aqueous solution of $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}$, pH is measured to be $9.95$. Calculate the solubility of calcium carbonate in water and show that the calculated value for the solubility product constant $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is $5\times10^{-9}$.
Blood contains calcium. Determine the maximum concentration of "free" calcium ions in the solution $(\mathrm{pH}=7.40,\ [\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]=0.022)$ given in 1.4.

problems.statement: Nitrogen in agricultural materials is often determined by the Kjeldahl method. The method involves a treatment of the sample with hot concentrated sulphuric acid, to convert organically bound nitrogen to ammonium ion. Concentrated sodium hydroxide is then added, and the ammonia formed is distilled into hydrochloric acid of known volume and concentration. The excess hydrochloric acid is then back-titrated with a standard solution of sodium hydroxide, to determine nitrogen in the sample.

parts.statement: $0.2515\ \mathrm{g}$ of a grain sample was treated with sulphuric acid, sodium hydroxide was then added and the ammonia distilled into $50.00\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ of $0.1010\ \mathrm{M}$ hydrochloric acid. The excess acid was back-titrated with $19.30\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ of $0.1050\ \mathrm{M}$ sodium hydroxide. Calculate the concentration of nitrogen in the sample, in percent by mass.

Calculate the pH of the solution which is titrated in 2.1 when $0\ \mathrm{cm}^3$, $9.65\ \mathrm{cm}^3$, $19.30\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ and $28.95\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ of sodium hydroxide have been added. Disregard any volume change during the reaction of ammonia gas with hydrochloric acid. $K_a$ for ammonium ion is $5.7\times10^{-10}$.
Draw the titration curve based on the calculations in b).
What is the pH transition range of the indicator which could be used for the back titration.

The Kjeldahl method can also be used to determine the molecular weight of amino acids. In a given experiment, the molecular weight of a naturally occurring amino acid was determined by digesting $0.2345\ \mathrm{g}$ of the pure acid and distilling ammonia released into $50.00\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ of $0.1010\ \mathrm{M}$ hydrochloric acid. A titration volume of $17.50\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ was obtained for the back titration with $0.1050\ \mathrm{M}$ sodium hydroxide.

Calculate the molecular weight of the amino acid based on one and two nitrogen groups in the molecule, respectively.

problems.statement: Sulphur forms many different compounds with oxygen and halogens (sulphur as the central atom). These compounds are mainly molecular, and many are easily hydrolysed in water.

parts.statement: Write Lewis structures for molecules $\mathrm{SCl_2}$, $\mathrm{SO_3}$, $\mathrm{SO_2ClF}$, $\mathrm{SF_4}$, and $\mathrm{SBrF_5}$.
Carefully draw the geometries of the 5 molecules. (Disregard small deviations from "ideal" angles.)

A compound, consisting of sulphur (one atom per molecule), oxygen and one or more atoms of the elements F, Cl, Br, and I, was examined. A small amount of the substance reacted with water. It was completely hydrolyzed without any oxidation or reduction, and all reaction products dissolved. $0.1\ \mathrm{M}$ solutions of a series of test reagents were added to separate small portions of a diluted solution of the substance.

Which ions are being tested for in the following tests?

i) Addition of $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ and $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$.

ii) Addition of $\mathrm{Ba(NO_3)_2}$.

iii) Adjustment to $\mathrm{pH}=7$ with $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and addition of $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$.

Write the equations for the possible reactions in the tests:

iv) Addition of $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ followed by $\mathrm{Ba(NO_3)_2}$ to an acid solution of the substance.

v) Addition of $\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}$.

In practice, the tests in 3.3 gave the following results:

i) A yellowish precipitate.

ii) No precipitate.

iii) No visible reaction.

iv) The main features were that the characteristic colour of permanganate disappeared, and a white precipitate was formed upon addition of $\mathrm{Ba(NO_3)_2}$.

v) No precipitate.

Write the formulas of the possible compounds, taking the results of these tests into account.

Finally, a simple quantitative analysis was undertaken:

$7.190\ \mathrm{g}$ of the substance was weighed out and dissolved in water to give $250.0\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ of a solution. To $25.00\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ of this solution, nitric acid and enough $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ was added to secure complete precipitation. After washing and drying the precipitate weighed $1.452\ \mathrm{g}$. Determine the formula of the compound.

Write the equation describing the reaction of the substance with water.

If you have not found the formula for the compound, use $\mathrm{SOClF}$.

problems.statement: Platinum(IV) oxide is not found in the nature, but it can be prepared in a laboratory. Solid platinum(IV) oxide is in equilibrium with platinum metal and oxygen gas at $1\ \mathrm{atm}$ ($=1.01325\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$) and $650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

parts.statement:
This suggests that the conditions on the Earth, when the minerals we know were formed, were:

| Alternative | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 1 | $p(\mathrm{O_2})=1\ \mathrm{atm},\ t=650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ |
| 2 | $p(\mathrm{O_2})<1\ \mathrm{atm},\ t<650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ |
| 3 | $p(\mathrm{O_2})>1\ \mathrm{atm},\ t<650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ |
| 4 | $p(\mathrm{O_2})<1\ \mathrm{atm},\ t>650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ |
| 5 | $p(\mathrm{O_2})>1\ \mathrm{atm},\ t>650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ |

Mark the most probable alternative 1–5 on the answer sheet. Please note that the marking of only one alternative will be accepted.
What are $\Delta G$ and $K_p$ for the formation of platinum(IV) oxide at oxygen pressure of $1\ \mathrm{atm}$ and temperature of $650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

The preparation of platinum(IV) oxide involves boiling of a solution which contains hexachloroplatinate(IV) ions with sodium carbonate. In this process $\mathrm{PtO_2\cdot nH_2O}$ is formed and this is in turn converted to platinum(IV) oxide upon subsequent filtering and heat treatment. In the following we assume $n=4$.

$\mathrm{PtO_2\cdot4H_2O}$ or $\mathrm{Pt(OH)_4\cdot2H_2O}$ can be dissolved in acids and strong bases.

Write the balanced equations for the preparation of platinum(IV) oxide according to the procedure given above.
Write the balanced equations for the dissolution of $\mathrm{PtO_2\cdot4H_2O}$ in both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.

Platinum is mainly found in the nature as the metal (in mixture or in alloying with other precious metals). Platinum is dissolved in aqua regia under the formation of hexachloroplatinate(IV) ions. Aqua regia is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids in proportion $3:1$, and of the nitrosylchloride ($\mathrm{NOCl}$) and the atomic chlorine which are formed upon the mixing. The latter is believed to be the active dissolving component.

The hexachloroplatinate(IV) ions can be precipitated as diammonium hexachloroplatinate(IV) and by thermal decomposition of this compound, finely powdered platinum and gaseous products are formed.

Write the balanced equations for the formation of aqua regia and its reaction with platinum.
Write the balanced equation of the thermal decomposition of diammonium hexachloroplatinate(IV) at elevated temperature.

From diammonium hexachloroplatinate(IV) we can prepare $\mathrm{Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$ which occurs in cis ($\Delta H_f^0=-467.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta G_f^0=-228.7\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) and trans ($\Delta H_f^0=-480.3\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta G_f^0=-222.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) form.

The occurrence of the isomers shows that $\mathrm{Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$ has geometry:

| Alternative | Geometry |
|---|---|
| 1 | Linear |
| 2 | Planar |
| 3 | Tetrahedral |
| 4 | Octahedral |

Mark the correct alternative 1–4 on the answer sheet.
Is the cis form or trans form thermodynamically more stable?

Platinum is used as a catalyst in modern automobiles. In the catalyst carbon monoxide ($\Delta H_f^0=-110.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta G_f^0=-137.3\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) reacts with oxygen to carbon dioxide ($\Delta H_f^0=-393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta G_f^0=-394.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).

Is the reaction spontaneous at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Choose 1 (yes) or 2 (no). Is the reaction 3 (endothermic) or 4 (exothermic)? Calculate $\Delta S^\circ$ for the reaction. Establish whether the entropy of the reaction system 5 (increases) or 6 (decreases).
Establish an expression for the temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant in this case.

The overall catalytic reaction is simple, whereas the reaction mechanism in the homogeneous phase is very complicated with a large number of reaction steps, and the course is difficult to control owing to a distinct chain character. With platinum as catalyst the significant reaction steps are: (i) adsorption of CO and adsorption/dissociation of $\mathrm{O_2}$ ($\Delta H=-259\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per mol CO + O), (ii) their activation ($105\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per mol CO + O) and (iii) the reaction and the desorption of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($\Delta H=21\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per mol $\mathrm{CO_2}$).

A one-dimensional energy-diagram for the platinum catalyzed oxidation of carbon monoxide to dioxide can be represented as:

![](p4-fig1)

Mark the correct alternative 1–4 on the answer sheet.

An optical active compound A ($\mathrm{C_{12}H_{16}O}$) shows amongst other a strong IR-absorption at $3000$–$3500\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and two medium signals at $1580$ and $1500\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The compound does not react with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-D). Upon treatment with $\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}$, A is oxidized and gives a positive iodoform reaction.

Ozonolysis of A (1. $\mathrm{O_3}$; 2. $\mathrm{Zn,H^+}$) gives B ($\mathrm{C_9H_{10}O}$) and C ($\mathrm{C_3H_6O_2}$). Both B and C give precipitation when treated with 2,4-D, and only C gives positive reaction with Tollens reagent. Nitration of B ($\mathrm{HNO_3/H_2SO_4}$) may give two mono-nitro compounds D and E, but in practical work only D is formed.

Acidification followed by heating of the product formed by the Tollens reaction on C gives compound F ($\mathrm{C_6H_8O_4}$). The compound gives no absorption in IR above $3100\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

parts.statement: Based on the above information draw the structure formula(e) for the compounds A–F and give the overall reaction scheme, including the (2,4-D) and the products of the Tollens and iodoform reactions.
Draw C in an R-configuration. Transform this into a Fischer projection formula and state whether it is a D or L configuration.

parts.statement:
When an ideal, monatomic gas expands reversibly from a volume $V_1$ to a volume $V_2$, a work

$$
w=-\int_{V_1}^{V_2}p\,dV
$$

is performed on the system by the surroundings. In this equation, $w$ is the work and $p$ is the pressure of the gas.

Determine the performed work when one mole ideal gas expands isothermally from $V_1=1.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ to $V_2=20.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ at the temperature $T=300.0\ \mathrm{K}$.

Given: The gas constant $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.
Determine how much heat must be added to the gas during the process given under 7.1.

The gas will perform less work in an adiabatic expansion than in an isothermal expansion. Is this because the adiabatic expansion is characterized by (check the square you think is most important):

| Alternative | Statement |
|---|---|
| 1 | The volume of the gas is constant |
| 2 | The expansion is always irreversible |
| 3 | No heat is supplied to the gas |

The cyclic process shown schematically in Figure 1 shows the four steps in a refrigeration system with an ideal gas as working medium. Identify the isothermal and adiabatic steps in the process. Here, $T_H$ and $T_C$ represent high and low temperature, respectively. Specify for each step whether it is adiabatic or isothermal.

![](p7-fig1)

sections.statement:
Work performed on the gas is

$$
w=-\int_{V_1}^{V_2}p\,dV=-RT\int_{V_1}^{V_2}\frac{dV}{V}=-RT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}
$$

$$
=-8{,}314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\times300\ \mathrm{K}\times\ln\frac{20.00}{1.00}=-7472\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}=-7.47\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

Because this is an isothermal expansion of an ideal monatomic gas, there is no change in internal energy. From the first law of thermodynamics, we then have that

$$
\Delta U=q+w=0,
$$

where $q$ is the amount of supplied heat and $w$ is performed work. This leads to

$$
q=-w=7.47\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
$$
3: No heat is supplied to the gas.

The shaded boxes in the native key select:

| Step | Isotherm | Adiabat |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Selected | |
| 2–3 | | Selected |
| 3–4 | Selected | |
| 4–1 | | Selected |

parts.statement:
An atom of ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ disintegrates by a series of $\alpha$-decays and $\beta^-$-decays until it becomes ${}^{206}\mathrm{Pb}$, which is stable.

i) How many $\alpha$-decays and how many $\beta^-$-decays does an atom starting as ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ undergo before it becomes stable?

ii) One of the following ten nuclides is formed from a series of disintegrations starting at ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$. Which one?

$$
{}^{235}\mathrm{U},\quad {}^{234}\mathrm{U},\quad {}^{228}\mathrm{Ac},\quad {}^{224}\mathrm{Ra},\quad {}^{224}\mathrm{Rn},\quad {}^{220}\mathrm{Rn},\quad {}^{215}\mathrm{Po},\quad {}^{212}\mathrm{Po},\quad {}^{212}\mathrm{Pb},\quad {}^{211}\mathrm{Pb}.
$$

In a thermal neutron-induced fission process, ${}^{235}\mathrm{U}$ reacts with a neutron and breaks up into energetic fragments and (normally) 2–3 new neutrons.

We consider one single fission event:

$$
{}^{235}\mathrm{U}+\mathrm{n}\longrightarrow{}{}^{137}\mathrm{Te}+X+2\mathrm{n}.
$$

Identify the fragment $X$.

The half-life of ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ is $4.5\times10^9$ years, the half-life of ${}^{235}\mathrm{U}$ is $7.0\times10^8$ years. Natural uranium consists of $99.28\%$ ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ and $0.72\%$ ${}^{235}\mathrm{U}$.

i) Calculate the ratio in natural U between the disintegration rates of these two uranium isotopes.

ii) A mineral contains 50 weight percent uranium. Calculate the disintegration rate of ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ in $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of this mineral.

We have the following radioactive sequence:

$$
{}^{97}\mathrm{Ru}\longrightarrow{}{}^{97}\mathrm{Tc}\longrightarrow{}{}^{97}\mathrm{Mo}\text{ (stable)}.
$$

Halflives: ${}^{97}\mathrm{Ru}$: $2.7$ days; ${}^{97}\mathrm{Tc}$: $2.6\times10^6$ years.

At $t=0$ a radioactive source containing only ${}^{97}\mathrm{Ru}$ has a disintegration rate of $1.0\times10^9\ \mathrm{Bq}$.

i) What is the total disintegration rate of the source at $t=6.0$ days?

ii) What is the total disintegration rate of the source at $t=6000$ years?

sections.statement:
i) 8 $\alpha$'s and 6 $\beta^-$'s (only $\alpha$'s gives ${}^{206}\mathrm{Os}$, to come from Os to Pb requires 6 $\beta^-$'s).

ii) ${}^{234}\mathrm{U}$, all other answers are incorrect.

i)

$$
D=\lambda N,\qquad \frac{D_1}{D_2}=\frac{\lambda_1N_1}{\lambda_2N_2}=\frac{\operatorname{abund.}(1)T_{1/2}(2)}{\operatorname{abund.}(2)T_{1/2}(1)}
$$

$$
=\frac{99.28\times7.0\times10^8}{0.72\times4.5\times10^9}=21.4.
$$

($0.047$ is also of course correct.)

ii)

$$
N=\frac{m}{\operatorname{AW}(U)}\times\operatorname{abundance}(238)\times N_A=\frac{500}{238.01}\times0.9928\times6.022\times10^{23}=1.26\times10^{24}.
$$

$$
D=\frac{N\ln2}{T_{1/2}}=\frac{1.26\times10^{24}\times\ln2}{4.5\times10^9\ \mathrm{y}\times3.16\times10^7\ \mathrm{s\,y^{-1}}}=6.1\times10^6\ \mathrm{Bq}.
$$

i) $\lambda=\ln2/2.7\ \mathrm{d}=0.26\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}$.

$$
D=D_0e^{-\lambda t}=1.0\times10^9\times e^{-(0.26\times6.0)}=2.1\times10^8\ \mathrm{Bq}.
$$

ii) Number of ${}^{97}\mathrm{Ru}$ atoms in the source:

$$
N=\frac{DT_{1/2}({}^{97}\mathrm{Ru})}{\ln2}=\frac{1.0\times10^9\ \mathrm{Bq}\times2.7\ \mathrm{d}\times24\ \mathrm{h\,d^{-1}}\times3600\ \mathrm{s\,h^{-1}}}{0.6931}=3.4\times10^{14}\text{ atoms}.
$$

When all ${}^{97}\mathrm{Ru}$ has disintegrated, these atoms have all become ${}^{97}\mathrm{Tc}$, and the disintegration rate of this nuclide is

$$
D=\frac{N\ln2}{T_{1/2}({}^{97}\mathrm{Tc})}=\frac{3.4\times10^{14}\times0.6931}{2.6\times10^6\ \mathrm{y}\times3.16\times10^7\ \mathrm{s\,y^{-1}}}=2.9\ \mathrm{Bq}.
$$
